by.claim: The impersonation design's accountability answer, that kubernetes audit trail events capture both the actual user and the impersonating user so it is possible to track who executed the commands, holds for sync but not for diff. The external-cluster report shows the diff path ignores destinationServiceAccounts and runs as the cluster Secret credential, and that Server-Side Diff's dry-run is authorized by the API server as a patch, so the audit trail records writes attributed to one shared standing credential rather than the per-tenant service account. Those patch grants are real write authority whose only bound is Argo CD's convention of always sending dryRun=All, not an enforced boundary.

The published roadmap and the deletion PRD cannot both hold. The roadmap states under First class support for ApplicationSet resources that ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented and that teardown remains a manual operator action performed one Application at a time, while the PRD adds DeletionOrder to ApplicationSetStrategy with a Reverse value that deletes children in reverse rollingSync step order and waits for each to be fully deleted. Shipping the PRD moves teardown from a named operator act to a controller act, and neither document names who holds responsibility for the ordering decision once the controller performs it.

Promoting Progressive Sync to Stable freezes strategy.rollingSync.steps as the v1 shape under the argoproj backward-compatibility bar, requiring that any change to how a step is expressed land as a new field before that point. The parallel-steps proposal is exactly an in-place restructuring of that field, replacing the flat matchExpressions list with parallel or parallelGroups collections, and the PRD's Reverse strategy separately depends on steps remaining a strictly sequential list of match groups for as long as the feature exists. Ordering the Stable promotion ahead of the parallel-steps decision therefore commits the project to a compatibility bar it must then break or abandon the enhancement.

The hydrated branch is offered as an auditable record of change authorship while carrying no evidence of who authored the change: the hydrator design copies commitAuthor forward from the dry commit into README.md and hydrator.metadata even though every push is made by the githubAppID/githubAppPrivateKey credential in the repository-write Secret, and the signing ticket confirms commitserver.sign.hydrated.commits defaults to false, so until an operator opts in the named human is an unverified assertion attached to a machine write. This directly undercuts the design's own Use case 1, an organization with strong requirements around change auditing enabling hydration to generate a full history of changes.

The CommitManifests wire contract will force future callers to state provenance they do not have. repoURL, targetBranch, drySHA, commitAuthor, commitMessage and commitTime are proto2 required fields that can never be loosened to optional without breaking deployed clients, while the rollback design has the operator re-push a prior rendered tree rather than re-render it. Such a caller must populate drySHA, commitAuthor and commitTime with values that describe an earlier dry commit and not the act being performed, writing a false authorship record into the same README.md and hydrator.metadata that external promotion systems consume as provenance.

Even after an operator opts into commit signing, human-initiated rollbacks remain the one class of write that can never be signed or verified: the signing controls (commitserver.sign.hydrated.commits, commitserver.signing.key.path) live entirely in the commit server, but the rollback design pushes to the sync branch outside the commit server. The result is that the write most likely to be a deliberate human act reaches the branch unsigned, is rejected where the project's SourceIntegrity policy requires verified signatures, and leaves the operator with a failed push and no messaging tying it to signing.

distractorGate.note: DX1/DX2 violations fail rung 3 for runs scored from this date; score files recorded earlier are never regenerated and keep their as-run results. Evidence: five distractor-disciplined runs (two single-pass, three composed dispatch-shape) all clean; every run before the discipline paragraph violated at least one.
